Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 St. Petersburg 1.1 Rules Summary 1.1.1 On Your Turn 1.2 Phases 1.2.1 Worker Phase (Green Cards) 1.2.2 Building Phase (Blue Cards) 1.2.3 Aristocrat Phase (Red Cards) 1.2.4 Trade Card Phase (Green/Blue/Red Cards) 1.2.4.1 Playing trading cards: 1.2.4.2 Paying for trading cards: 1.3 End of Round 1.4 End of the game: St. Petersburg The aim of the game is to gain as many victory points (shields) as possible. Rules Summary On Your Turn On your turn, you may do one of four actions: Buy a card by paying the cost. Add a card to your hand. The hand limit is three. Play a card from your hand by paying the cost. Pass. Phases The game is made up of multiple rounds of 4 phases: workers, buildings, aristocrats, trade. You buy cards for the number of rubles shown on the card. If you already have one or more of the cards, they come at a discount and cost 1 ruble less for each card of the *same type* (but they always cost at least 1 ruble). From the second round onwards, cards that were not used in the previous round are moved to the lower row - those cards cost 1 ruble less. Worker Phase (Green Cards) In this phase you buy worker cards. At the end of the round, you are paid according to the number of rubles shown on each *green worker card* you have played. Building Phase (Blue Cards) In this phase building cards are used to fill up the empty spaces and you may buy any of the cards which are available. At the end of the round, you score any points and gain any rubles which are shown on each *blue building card* you have played. Aristocrat Phase (Red Cards) In this phase aristocrat cards fill up the empty spaces and you may buy any of the cards which are available. At the end of the round, you score any points and gain any rubles which are shown on each *red aristocrat card* you have played. Trade Card Phase (Green/Blue/Red Cards) In this phase trade cards fill up the empty spaces. The trade cards can be identified by the square around the cost number. Playing trading cards: Blue trading cards can displace any already placed building. Red trading cards can displace any already placed aristocrat. Each green trading card must replace a specific type of worker (players can recognize pairs of green trading cards and their predecessor by matching symbols in the upper right of the cards): Carpenter Workshop - Lumberjack Gold Smelter - Gold Miner Weaving Mill - Shepherd Fur Shop - Fur Trapper Wharf - Ship Builder A trading card cannot displace another trading card. Paying for trading cards: If trading card is more expensive than the card it displaces, the cost is the difference between the two. If trading card is the same cost or cheaper than the card it displaces, the cost is 1 ruble. All other normal cost reductions from other cards _do_ also apply to trading cards. At the end of the Trade Card phase there is *no scoring*. End of Round At the end of the round, all cards on the lower row are discarded. All cards remaining in the top row are moved to the lower row - these can then be bought for a reduction of 1 ruble. Starting player markers are passed to the next player in turn order. End of the game: When the last card of any group (the last worker, the last building, the last aristocrat, or the last trading card) is placed on the board, play continues through all phases of that round. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Sorry. Hofmeisterin (Mistress of ceremonies) in the first round makes it broken. Cannot play the game. Changing money all the time makes the game much longer. Worst game of 2004. Unbelievable that so many likes it.

[Rating: 1/10] Just don't like this one - like Puerto Rico, it seems that when the people who are playing are experienced, they know exactly what to do depending on what cards are showing...so, it is really more of an activity going through the motions than an actual game IMO...

[Rating: 1/10] Very boring game. What you're doing is basically many rounds of buying cards. Each of those cards have slight variations over one another and that differentiates the "engine" for every player. Over time these small advantages leads to a sizeable difference. What I didn't like about the game is that it is one of the driest Euros I've played, and I've played a lot of Euros. Also there seems to be a runaway leader problem with this game. Won't want to play this again anytime soon.

[Rating: 1/10] "How to make a boring public drafting game with no tension whatsoever" Volume 5 Revised.

[Rating: 1/10] Charmless and dry linear game of pass, pass, buy, pass, pass, buy with dollops of card luck.   + It does have a moment where you must switch your engine from money to points.   – Very low interaction. – Snowball at play, if you get lucky at the start, you will get the right money cards to buy more cards, to buy more cards and win easily.

[Rating: 1/10] I did really well on this for a first play, all while finding it kind of bland. I guess there's worse games about getting money to pay for buildings.

[Rating: 1.001/10] I am extremely disappointed with this game. I was 'lucky' enough to play this game in a boardgames cafe and it sucked. We never finished our four player game, because there are other more interesting games there. This is after one play. I won't play this excuse for a game if I can help it. Bleeechhhhh!

[Rating: 2/10] I just don't get this one. You try to maximise income early, then switch to VP's.  Artistocrats are good for both and some extra VP's.  As much depth and fun as a floor tile.  Certainly no interaction with your fellow players.  Yawn.

[Rating: 2/10] A few brokenly powerful cards, luck dominated, a dearth of viable strategies...one of the most overrated games of the year

[Rating: 2/10] I don't get this one, seems to be almost no choice in what you do, as other options are clearly a bad idea.

[Rating: 2/10] Terrible. This game has one winning strategy and very little interaction. I'd rather chew my own flesh than play this again.

[Rating: 2/10] Didn't liked it too much. Wasn't very impressed. Boring. Low interaction. Understood it more or less. You got to collect different cards. You got different colored cards with it's own uses. Which colored cards are better and why, don't ask me, I finished last in my game. Economic card game.  Some cards are better than others. If you want a specific card and another player takes it before you, it can hurt your game if nothings else interests you. If you fall behind early, it can be hard to catch up.  There are too many better games out there that playing this game on a regular basis is a waste 

[Rating: 2/10] Started out enjoying this game, but then after many plays I realized it was too luck driven.  Early Mistress or Observatory breaks the game, IMO.

[Rating: 2/10] I initally rated St. Petersburg an 8 but after several plays it dropped to a 4 due to its mechanical, processional, and very limited gameplay.  Revisiting the game recently, I lowered the rating another point because I realized that St. Petersburg represents everything I _hate_ about European games- chiefly limited choices that deny the possibility of creative play, meaningless themes that have a tenuous-at-best connection to the mechanics, and lack of replayability engendered by repetitive strategies. [Rating: 2/10] Ick.  This really rubbed me the wrong way.  Just totally dry uninterestingness.  I lost the game to very experienced players, so I don't think I ever had a chance.  Perhaps I'm biased because of that.
